title: Jude and the Hymn
premise: Lena Vane hosts a late-night call-in show from the Hollow Pines boarding house, where the callers are residents who died the previous week and the house itself keeps count of its doors. When she plays back her sleep recordings, a second voice answers questions she never asked aloud—the voice of the hymn's composer, who was lynched by the town's founders and buried beneath the property. As developer papers circulate to sell the land, Lena must learn the hymn's final verse from the dead without singing along herself, because every voice that joins the song becomes one of the counted doors. In the end, Lena refuses to sign, teaches the verse to the last living resident—a dying old woman who chooses to sing it freely—and the house opens all its doors at once, freeing the trapped dead while leaving Lena alone on an empty lot with only a radio that still receives one final call: her own.
about_author: Hazel Sterling is the pen name of a former overnight radio producer who spent six years working graveyard shifts in small-market stations across Appalachia. She writes horror about places that remember what people want forgotten.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. She runs her 2 a.m. call-in show from the boarding house parlor; tonight's caller describes his own funeral in detail. She checks the door count—eleven doors, twelve locks—and tells herself it's a prank. Emotional beat: controlled denial, the comfort of routine stretched thin.

chapters.title: The Roster
chapters.summary: Lena cross-references last week's obituaries against her caller log: every regular listener died within seven days. The house's hallway has grown one door longer. POV shifts briefly to Marcus, the handyman, who admits he heard singing under the floorboards. Beat: dread replacing skepticism.

chapters.title: Sleep Study
chapters.summary: Lena records herself sleeping after weeks of exhaustion. Playback reveals a second voice answering questions she never asked—patient, formal, waiting. It says her name correctly, which no one in Hollow Pines does. Beat: intimate violation; the self made strange.

chapters.title: Doors Counted
chapters.summary: Marcus and Lena inventory the house: doors that open onto the same room, a basement stair with forty-one steps down and forty-two up. They find the original deed naming the property 'Hymn Lot.' Beat: uneasy alliance forming between two people who don't trust each other.

chapters.title: Caller Number Nine
chapters.summary: A live caller asks Lena to read a verse of an old hymn on air. She reads it; every light in the house dims in sequence like held breath. The caller thanks her and hangs up mid-word. Beat: first taste of power—and cost.

chapters.title: The Papers
chapters.summary: Developer's agent Delia Marsh arrives with buyout documents for the last three residents. Signing means demolition; demolition means whatever is under the lot gets dug up. Lena realizes the dead callers aren't haunting—they're petitioning. Beat: stakes sharpened by mundane greed.

chapters.title: Verse One
chapters.summary: In the sleep recording, the second voice begins teaching: the hymn's first verse, sung once, slowly. Lena hums it absentmindedly while making coffee and the kitchen faucet runs backward for an hour. Beat: curiosity punished; rules half-learned.

chapters.title: What Marcus Knows
chapters.summary: Marcus's POV. His grandmother sang this hymn; her sister joined the choir in 1953 and was never seen again. He gives Lena a hymnal with the final verse torn out. Beat: loyalty offered alongside a warning—he'll help, but not past a line he won't name.

chapters.title: The Founders' Ledger
chapters.summary: County archive chapter. Lena finds the ledger: in 1911, the town hanged a Black composer named Ezekiel Reed on the lot and buried him beneath the foundation, then built the boarding house over him as a lock. Beat: cold historical horror; justice deferred a century.

chapters.title: Twelve Locks
chapters.summary: Lena counts again: eleven doors, thirteen locks now. Each resident who signs the papers adds a lock. Mrs. Okafor, the last holdout, signs 'pending.' That night the sleep voice says, 'One more and I can speak plainly.' Beat: the trap revealed—she's been negotiating, not haunting.

chapters.title: Delia's Offer
chapters.summary: Delia returns, sympathetic, revealing she grew up hearing the hymn too and wants the lot cleared before it clears itself. She offers Lena money and a way out. Lena almost takes it. Beat: temptation; belonging versus escape.

chapters.title: Verse Two
chapters.summary: The second voice teaches verse two, and this time it explains the rule: sing along and you become a door. Lena transcribes without voicing it, lips moving silent. Marcus catches her practicing and nearly leaves. Beat: discipline as survival; friendship strained.

chapters.title: The Choir Rehearsal
chapters.summary: At midnight all the dead callers join a single broadcast, singing verses one and two in harmony while the living residents sleepwalk into the hall. Lena cuts the transmitter; the silence afterward is worse. Beat: awe curdling into terror.

chapters.title: Mrs. Okafor's Room
chapters.summary: POV: Mrs. Okafor, dying, lucid. She remembers Ezekiel Reed—her grandfather's friend—and has kept the torn verse memorized for sixty years, refusing to give it up or use it. She offers Lena a trade: the verse for a promise. Beat: grief and inheritance.

chapters.title: The Promise
chapters.summary: Okafor's price: the song must be finished by someone who chooses it, freely, knowing the cost—not tricked or coerced. Lena realizes the house doesn't want a singer; it wants a witness. Beat: thematic pivot toward consent and justice.

chapters.title: Lockout
chapters.summary: Delia forces the sale through probate; signing day is set. The house responds—doors seal, phones die, the transmitter broadcasts on its own. Marcus breaks his line: he stays. Beat: siege pressure; loyalty chosen under fear.

chapters.title: Under the Floorboards
chapters.summary: Lena descends the forty-two steps and finds the root cellar: a grave, a rusted harmonica, and Ezekiel Reed himself—not a monster, a man worn to patience. He asks her only to listen. Beat: the antagonist revealed as the wronged party.

chapters.title: Ezekiel's Testimony
chapters.summary: Reed tells the whole story: the hymn was a map home for people the town erased, and they buried the composer to bury the route. Every death since has been the house asking to be unlocked. Beat: moral inversion complete; the horror was the town.

chapters.title: Signing Day
chapters.summary: Delia arrives with the final signature page. Okafor, hours from death, signs—but writes a condition into the margin. The house accepts it. Doors begin opening on their own, one per hour. Beat: climax ignition; the countdown made literal.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: In the parlor, Okafor sings the final verse—freely, eyes open—while Lena holds the microphone so the broadcast carries it. The dead answer in harmony. Okafor dies smiling as the twelfth lock falls. Beat: catharsis; grief transfigured into release.

chapters.title: All Doors Open
chapters.summary: The house exhales. Walls fold outward, the dead walk out into dawn and dissolve, Reed's grave surfaces and is finally marked with his name. Delia, changed, tears up the sale. Beat: resolution; justice outside any courtroom.

chapters.title: Sign-Off
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Lena hosts one final broadcast from an empty lot. At 2 a.m., the board lights: a caller with her own voice, thanking her for listening. She signs off, keeps the lights on out of habit, and walks away counting nothing. Beat: quiet aftermath; belonging found in witness, not walls.
